say: Welcome—this infographic follows one hotel-improvement project from public research to local evidence, then into a proposal, slides and a meeting draft. We're working across arrival and rooms, facilities, and food and service rather than choosing separate topics.

You'll use Researcher to look outward, Analyst to test one shared approach against a fictional workbook, and a workspace to bring the material together. The important thread isn't producing lots of polished documents; it's preserving what the evidence supports, what challenges it and what we still don't know.
welcome.ask: Why would a convincing public example still need checking against this hotel's own data?
welcome.watch: Walk the infographic from Researcher to Analyst to Workspaces; emphasise the difference between a sourced idea and proof of local success.

say: These four cards establish our evidence discipline: fictional training data only, public research isn't proof of local fit, claims need sources, and missing values stay missing. Never add real guest or staff details to make the exercise feel more realistic.

For public findings, keep the source and publication date; for hotel figures, keep the workbook sheet and record. A blank isn't zero, and a proposed improvement doesn't come with an invented owner, budget, deadline or promised outcome just because the writing sounds confident.
needs.ask: How would treating an unrecorded wait as zero distort an improvement assessment?
needs.watch: Pause on Missing stays missing; ensure learners understand this is a data-interpretation rule, not merely a formatting preference.

say: You're a Hotel Operations Improvement Team Member investigating the three connected areas shown on the left. The goals on the right are to find credible ideas, test the class approach against hotel evidence and reach a proposal that people can discuss.

Read the scope before starting: Reservation Journey isn't part of this session, and we're not approving budgets or a hotel-wide strategy. The report, assessment, proposal, slides and agenda are tools for informed discussion, so keep investigation separate from decisions the workshop hasn't authorised.
story.ask: Which of the three operating areas could affect another area's guest experience, and what would you need to investigate?
story.watch: Point to the explicit Reservation Journey exclusion; keep the class on the shared daily-guest-experience problem.

say: Download 02_Hotel_Operations_Improvement.xlsx from the single starter-file card and save it in your working folder. It contains Arrival & Rooms, Facilities, and Food & Service, and it controls the hotel numbers we'll use throughout this project.

The report, assessment and proposal aren't pre-made answers to download; you'll create them during the activities. Keep this original workbook available for repeated checks, because a later summary or presentation needs to trace its figures back to actual sheets and records rather than to another generated paragraph.
files.ask: Which file is the authority for a hotel figure if a later report gives a different number?
files.watch: Confirm the exact workbook filename, including 02_; don't send learners looking for additional starter reports.

say: Open Researcher under Agents & Skills and send the first full prompt, following the animated selection and typing. This stage needs no file attachments: we're looking for credible public approaches across the three operating areas, with evidence, conditions, limitations and source dates.

Wait for the complete report rather than stopping at the first appealing idea. As you read, distinguish what a source actually supports from opinion or a suggestion, and keep the questions that need local data visible instead of assuming the research has already solved our hotel's problem.
p1.ask: Which finding comes with a named source and a stated limitation or condition?
p1.watch: Use the complete Copy prompt text, not the shortened animation; allow Researcher to finish without inventing findings while learners wait.

say: The nine fields on screen show what the saved research should retain, including evidence, conditions, suggested measures and unanswered questions. Copy the whole Researcher answer into Word and save it as Hotel_Improvement_Research_Report.docx.

Keep the source names and publication dates rather than shortening the report into unsupported tips. This document will be added to Analyst and then the workspace, so losing those details now makes every later comparison harder; the lesson page itself doesn't save your report for you.
savereport.ask: Does your saved report retain the source and date behind each major finding?
savereport.watch: Pause at Copy the file name; verify learners save the complete answer in Word rather than only copying the on-screen field labels.

say: Use the five interactive checks only after looking in your report: source, date, evidence, conditions and limitations. Open the linked sources and confirm that the findings genuinely say what the report attributes to them.

The progress bar reveals the class approach after all five checks, but the ticks are your record of verification, not a test the page performs for you. If something is missing, ask Researcher to supply the source, date or condition and inspect it before marking that check complete.
checks.ask: Which check would fail if the report listed attractive ideas but didn't explain the supporting evidence?
checks.watch: Don't tick the five cards on learners' behalf to bypass the gate; give time to open sources and correct missing information.

say: Let's pause with the challenge and research stages coloured in and Analyst highlighted next. You've saved a report and checked its public sources, so the question now changes from what others have tried to what our hotel evidence can support.

There's no new prompt at this checkpoint. If you haven't opened the sources behind the findings, use the five-checks link before moving on; a credible-looking report isn't enough when we're about to use its ideas to interpret local data.
cp1.ask: Did opening a public source confirm the report's finding, or reveal a qualification worth keeping?
cp1.watch: Use the checkpoint's five-checks link for incomplete verification; explain the outward-to-inward shift before advancing.

say: Our shared approach is a daily readiness huddle, where front desk, housekeeping, maintenance and food service compare arrivals, ready rooms, unavailable facilities and stock gaps. Everyone tests that same approach rather than selecting whichever idea the research made most appealing.

Open 02_Hotel_Operations_Improvement.xlsx and explore all three sheets before using Analyst. Look for pressure events, counterexamples, blank waits, unfinished incidents and potentially inconsistent notes; knowing where those records sit helps you judge an assessment instead of accepting a conclusion you can't trace.
approach.ask: Which sheet contains a counterexample or missing value that a fair huddle assessment must retain?
approach.watch: Confirm the five checks have unlocked this step; use the sheet cards to orient learners without inventing workbook figures.

say: Open Analyst and add both 02_Hotel_Operations_Improvement.xlsx and Hotel_Improvement_Research_Report.docx before sending the second prompt. The prompt uses the shorter workbook name Hotel_Operations_Improvement.xlsx, but the actual file to attach is the supplied 02_ version.

We're asking for evidence that supports or challenges testing the daily readiness huddle, plus gaps, dependencies, a baseline and a success measure. Compare the named sheets and records with the workbook, and don't let an association become a claim that the huddle caused an outcome.
p2.ask: Can you find a supporting record and a challenging record behind Analyst's assessment?
p2.watch: Check both attachments and the exact 02_ workbook filename; do not bypass the five-check gate or supply a made-up local conclusion.

say: Copy the assessment into Word and save Hotel_Approach_Assessment.docx, keeping the fields shown here. Check the cited sheet and record, supporting and contradictory evidence, missing information, baseline and success measure rather than saving the status alone.

The four statuses describe whether an approach is worth testing, not whether success is guaranteed. Relevant to test, Possibly relevant, Not supported and Cannot assess all need reasoning, and Cannot assess is appropriate when the evidence needed for a judgement simply isn't recorded.
assessment.ask: Does the assigned status follow from the cited records, including the contradictory or missing evidence?
assessment.watch: Point to the four status pills; give learners time to open the workbook locations before saving their checked assessment.

say: The checkpoint now marks the local assessment stage complete and highlights Workspaces next. You should have the original workbook, a checked research report and an assessment that preserves both support and counterexamples.

Let's pause without starting another prompt and ask whether every hotel claim has a traceable sheet and record. If a contradicting record disappeared from the assessment, bring it back before the handoff; combining documents won't repair evidence we've already lost.
cp2.ask: Can you still see the strongest counterexample alongside the evidence supporting a small test?
cp2.watch: Check the three-file handoff is ready; use the highlighted workspace stage to explain why those files now belong together.

say: Follow the cursor to Workspaces in the left menu and choose New workspace. The mock then leads toward the build screen, where we'll create the shared place for our research report, workbook and assessment.

Use the equivalent controls in your own Copilot if the screens differ from the illustration. At this point we're opening the place where the evidence will come together, not generating conclusions yet, so keep those three saved files ready for the next step.
wsopen.ask: Have you reached the new-workspace build screen with your three checked files available?
wsopen.watch: Allow for menu differences; distinguish selecting New workspace from the later Create workspace action.

say: Name the workspace Hotel Improvement and choose a colour, following the highlights in the build mock. Add members if you're practising as a team, then use the plus control to add your three files before selecting Create workspace.

Those files are Hotel_Improvement_Research_Report.docx, 02_Hotel_Operations_Improvement.xlsx and Hotel_Approach_Assessment.docx. Confirm the actual content rather than treating the illustrated file chips or peer as items the lesson has added for you; solo practice is fine when you're working alone.
wsbuild.ask: Do the three selected files represent external research, original hotel evidence and the checked local assessment?
wsbuild.watch: Pause at the file picker and compare exact filenames; don't require real colleague details or an invitation for solo learners.

say: Inside the new workspace, check its name and the three entries in Content before ticking the checklist. The cursor also points out Invite at the top right, while the plus beside Content is where additional files can be added.

Invite a peer if that's appropriate for your exercise, or mark that you're practising alone. The ticks should describe your own workspace, not just what the mock shows, because the next prompts need the complete evidence set rather than an empty shell with the right name.
wscheck.ask: Are all three actual files visible in Content, and are you working with a peer or practising solo?
wscheck.watch: Let learners verify their own Content panel before ticking; distinguish a real optional peer invitation from the synthetic person illustrated.

say: Open Message Copilot inside Hotel Improvement and send the first workspace prompt. We're checking what each of the three files contributes, then bringing external findings, supporting hotel evidence, counterexamples and gaps into one view.

Inspect every hotel-data statement for an exact sheet and record, date, period or ID that you can find in the workbook. Combining sources should make differences easier to see, not erase them, and missing values must remain missing rather than turning into invented figures or explanations.
wp1.ask: Does the combined context check preserve a counterexample and show where its record is located?
wp1.watch: Confirm learners are inside Hotel Improvement with all three files; compare the live response with actual workbook locations.

say: Use the next workspace prompt to form a Final Conclusions page from the evidence already collected. It asks for three to five conclusions, separating verified findings, cautious interpretations, contradictions and unresolved questions.

Check that each conclusion carries Strong support, Partial support, Not supported or Cannot assess, with source names, publication dates and workbook locations retained. The labels should make confidence inspectable, not conceal the reasoning, especially where public research and local hotel evidence disagree or cannot establish an outcome.
wp2.ask: Which conclusion has only partial support, and what prevents you from treating it as strongly established?
wp2.watch: Distinguish these conclusion labels from Analyst's earlier testing statuses; do not supply a predetermined winning conclusion.

say: Now turn the checked conclusions into Hotel_Improvement_Proposal.docx using the third workspace prompt. Look for the guest problem, selected approach, research and hotel evidence, then a small reversible pilot with baseline, measures, dependencies, risks and missing information.

Read it as material for operational discussion rather than an approved programme. The proposal must keep evidence apart from inference and avoid inventing funding, owners, dates or guaranteed results; save the output with the exact filename so the later review and presentation refer to the right document.
wp3.ask: What makes the proposed pilot reversible, and which condition still needs discussion before anyone could run it?
wp3.watch: Confirm the proposal is saved as Hotel_Improvement_Proposal.docx; stop if wording presents unapproved funding, assignments or outcomes as facts.

say: This review is mandatory even if the proposal reads beautifully. Send the fourth workspace prompt to compare Hotel_Improvement_Proposal.docx with the research report, assessment and workbook, and ask a peer to review it if you can.

Check the exact corrections, especially vanished contradictions, blanks turned into zeros, timing described as cause or recommendations presented as approvals. Fix the issues and inspect the final Ready for presentation or Needs correction judgement; a polished draft isn't ready until the evidence and wording survive this review.
wp4.ask: Which exact sentence needed correction, and what original evidence justified the change?
wp4.watch: Do not skip this step for time; ensure corrections are made, not merely listed, and retain solo review when collaboration is unavailable.

say: Let's pause with the workspace, conclusions and proposal-review stages marked complete, and presentation highlighted next. There are two moves left, but they depend on the reviewed proposal rather than a new round of unsupported claims.

Check your actual review outcome before continuing: Ready for presentation means something different from Needs correction. If issues remain, return to the proposal first; the checkpoint is a navigation pause, not permission to put unresolved figures or overconfident language onto slides.
cp3.ask: Is your corrected proposal ready for presentation, and what evidence supports that judgement?
cp3.watch: Ask for the real review outcome before advancing; don't assume the completed graphic means corrections have been resolved.

say: Send the fifth workspace prompt to create Hotel_Improvement_Proposal.pptx from the verified proposal. The six-slide structure moves from challenge and research through hotel evidence, contradictions and gaps to the small pilot and operational questions.

The page tells you to continue while the deck is being made, rather than wait in this conversation. When it becomes available in your workspace, check its sources, dates, workbook locations and cautious status language against the proposal; visual polish must not quietly remove uncertainty.
wp5.ask: Which slide needs to preserve the contradictory or missing evidence instead of presenting only the strongest case?
wp5.watch: Don't hold the class waiting for deck generation; move to the next step, then remind learners to inspect the completed six-slide file.

say: Start a new chat within this same workspace before sending the meeting-invite prompt, especially while the presentation is still being made. Ask for a subject, short invitation and thirty-minute agenda referring to Hotel_Improvement_Proposal.docx and Hotel_Improvement_Proposal.pptx.

Check the five, ten, ten and five-minute sections for challenge, evidence, pilot discussion and decisions. This is only a draft: add appropriate recipients, date and time yourself, and review the wording before any separate sending action; the workshop page doesn't send the invitation.
wp6.ask: Which agenda section gives peers room to challenge the pilot's risks and missing evidence?
wp6.watch: Ensure learners select New inside the workspace, not a chat outside it; emphasise the draft-only boundary and thirty-minute total.

say: Here are the same eight prompts: Researcher and Analyst first, then six inside Hotel Improvement. Download HotelImprovement-copilot-prompts.txt or use the individual copy buttons if you want to repeat part of the workflow.

Keep the prompts with the correct files and the shared daily readiness huddle approach rather than treating each card as an unrelated trick. The pack preserves instructions, not verified answers, so future use still needs the source, workbook and proposal checks that made today's handoffs meaningful.
prompts.ask: Which prompt would you return to if a proposal had lost a contradictory workbook record?
prompts.watch: Point out the two agent prompts versus six workspace prompts; clarify that the text download does not save learners' generated documents.

say: You've followed one evidence trail from public ideas through local testing to a proposal, six-slide presentation and meeting draft. The recap names the four skills, but the useful habit is keeping research, original hotel records and your interpretation distinguishable all the way through.

Pick a future problem where a small, well-evidenced test would be more sensible than a confident large promise. Keep the source-and-date checks, preserve missing information and own the judgement yourself; the Hospitality hub and Researcher learning link are here when you're ready to continue.
learned.ask: What small improvement question would you investigate next, and what local evidence would you need before proposing a pilot?
learned.watch: Invite a non-sensitive next-use idea; remind learners to check any deck still finishing before closing the workshop.
